strengths: Applies PINNs and its variants on a new real-world problem.
Provides details of the model architecture and the loss functions used in proposed PI-RGSM framework.
The problem of predicting river-canal groundwater seepage is interesting and is very important for a number of scientific applications.
The proposed method of enforcing hard-constraints is interesting.
The paper effectively applies physics-informed neural networks to model groundwater seepage, enhancing model interpretability and physical consistency.
By integrating hard constraints, the models reduce reliance on labeled data, making them suitable for scenarios with limited observational data.
The models achieve promising predictive performance.
automating the analysis of groundwater dynamics seems to be a useful application for machine learning.
weaknesses: The overall evaluation of the paper is weak. The paper mentions (in lines 167-169) that the main challenges in PINNs are the gradient pathologies with multiple loss terms, and the tedious nature of adjusting the trade-off hyper-parameters between these different terms. There is a rich body of work that addresses these challenges in PINNs, and should be used as baselines for comparison. Here are some of them: [1, 2, 3, 4]
Lack of comparison with methods that can enforce hard boundary constraints [5] in PINNs.

The “Input feature fusion” concept introduced in the paper is similar to the Neural Operators [6, 7, 8], where the ML model learns a family of PDEs instead of one single instantiation of a PDE. Therefore, the proposed PG-RGSM architecture seems like a simpler variant of the DeepONet [7] architecture, where both the coefficients and the spatio-temporal inputs are combined into one model instead of having a separate branch and trunk networks. Comparing against neural operators like DeepONets would further improve the paper.
The paper is poorly organized and lacks clarity, with essential content relegated to the appendix, leaving the main text insufficiently self-contained.
Although applying PINNs to groundwater seepage is relatively novel within the specific application area, the paper contributes little in terms of new machine learning techniques.
The model relies on manual tuning of hyperparameters (e.g., loss weights, threshold $H_{EC}$), but the paper lacks experiments analyzing the impact of these parameters.
The paper fails to compare the proposed method with existing machine learning models for groundwater seepage.

(clarity/novelty) The authors claim they introduce self-supervised PINNs, but I fail to comprehend how these models are more self-supervised than the original PINNs. The proposed models seem to use have an additional scaling and shift on top of the additional inputs compared to the baseline PINN, but I do not see how this makes these models self-supervised. Specifically, the training objective still relies on minimizing the residual of the governing PDE, similar to standard PINNs. The addition of scaling and shifting parameters does not fundamentally change the reliance on the PDE for supervision. A more detailed explanation of how the proposed modifications enhance the self-supervised nature of the model is needed.

(novelty) This model fails to cite any relevant related work in the main paper. I noticed there is a related work section in the appendix, but that does not suffice. During reading I had the impression this is the only paper applying deep learning in the field of hydrogeology, which is obviously not the case. Furthermore, the main paper should discuss how the proposed method compares to existing methods. A thorough comparison with prior work, especially in the context of incorporating physical constraints into neural networks, is crucial for establishing the novelty of the proposed approach.

(quality/clarity) I could not find information on how the baseline PINN was trained. E.g. section 2.2 mentions the different hyper-parameters in the loss function, but I could not find any information on what hyper-parameters were used or how they were found. Without details on the hyperparameter tuning process, such as the range of values explored and the criteria used for selection, the results cannot be properly evaluated or reproduced. The lack of a systematic approach to hyperparameter optimization raises concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the baseline model.

(quality) Each model is compared to a single baseline PINN. I strongly doubt that there are no stronger baselines to compare against (e.g. regular networks, non-ML methods, ...). Furthermore, the performance of the baseline PINN is so poor that it seems as if something went wrong during training (assuming a random model would achieve an R^2 of 0). Also, there are no error bars to indicate the consistency of the compared model(s). The absence of stronger baselines and error bars undermines the validity of the experimental results. A comparison with established numerical methods or other machine learning approaches would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the proposed models.

(significance/novelty) I fail to find a technical contribution that would be of interest to the machine learning community. The PINN modifications are ad‑hoc solutions for the equations at hand, and I can't imagine that this general idea has not been applied before. For an example of how physical constraints have been embedded in the architecture in the context of hydrology, I can refer to [1], but there are probably many more. The lack of a clear and novel technical contribution limits the impact of the work on the broader machine learning research landscape. The authors should clearly articulate the unique aspects of their approach and highlight its potential advantages over existing methods.
